tagline: The old highway through Halifax leads toward a fork of rivers
intro: Mountain Road leads through Vernon Hill into Halifax, where the highway passes the county courthouse before crossing the Banister River below Banister Lake. Farther east, Scottsburg Road reaches Staunton River State Park at the meeting of the Dan and Staunton rivers.

The route through Halifax carries an older highway identity: State Route 360 follows the former alignment of U.S. 360. The U.S. highway moved to a course through South Boston, sharing much of that route with U.S. 58.

Driving east from the Pittsylvania County line, follow Mountain Road through Vernon Hill to Halifax. State Route 360 joins Main Street, then continues east as Bethel Road across the Banister. At the junction with U.S. 360 west of Scottsburg, the onward road becomes State Route 344. It passes through Scottsburg and ends at the river park.

moments.title: Mountain Road Historic District
moments.text: Along State Route 360, the Mountain Road Historic District brings together houses, churches, a parish hall and a Masonic hall from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Its buildings include the 1828 Masonic Lodge, the 1831 Methodist Church and St. John’s Episcopal Church of 1844. Dabney Cosby, Jr. designed St. John’s and several earlier houses in the district. The district entered the National Register in 1983.

moments.title: Halifax
moments.text: The courthouse has a road number at its edges: State Route 349, Edmunds Boulevard, runs along two sides of the Halifax County courthouse. Dabney Cosby designed and built the courthouse in 1838–1839. The two-story brick building has a T-shaped plan and a portico with four Ionic columns. It belongs to the larger Town of Halifax Court House Historic District, whose buildings extend from the early nineteenth century into the mid-twentieth. That district includes mills as well as government buildings, houses and churches.
moments.notice: Look for the courthouse’s two-story portico and four Ionic columns.

moments.title: Staunton River State Park
moments.text: The park at the meeting of the Dan and Staunton rivers has changed with the water. The Civilian Conservation Corps built most of its buildings and facilities, and it opened in 1936 as one of Virginia’s original six state parks. In 1952, completion of the John H. Kerr Dam and formation of Buggs Island Lake flooded part of the park. The park is an International Dark Sky Park. The Staunton is also called the Roanoke River, but locally the name remains Staunton, pronounced “Stanton.” Its historic district includes cabins built in 1934–1936 and picnic shelters from the park’s early years.
